   102	/// Generate a patch and fold it into a manifest.
   103	///
   104	/// `existing` is the manifest currently published, if any. Because schema 1
   105	/// only supports patching *to the latest release*, a manifest describing an
   106	/// older version is replaced rather than merged — its patches reconstruct an
   107	/// artifact that is no longer current. A manifest for the same version has the
   108	/// new upgrade path added alongside the ones already there, which is what lets a
   109	/// release publish several `from` versions by calling this repeatedly.
   110	pub fn build_release(
   111	    req: &ReleaseRequest<'_>,
   112	    key: &SigningKey,
   113	    existing: Option<Manifest>,
   114	) -> Result<(Manifest, PatchSummary)> {
   115	    if req.from_version == req.version {
   116	        return Err(Error::Request(format!(
   117	            "cannot patch {} to itself",
   118	            req.version
   119	        )));
   120	    }
   121	    for (label, path) in [
   122	        ("previous installer", req.previous_installer),
   123	        ("new installer", req.new_installer),
   124	    ] {
   125	        if !path.is_file() {
   126	            return Err(Error::Request(format!(
   127	                "{label} {} does not exist",
   128	                path.display()
   129	            )));
   130	        }
   131	    }
   132	
   133	    if let Some(parent) = req.patch_out.parent() {
   134	        if !parent.as_os_str().is_empty() {
   135	            std::fs::create_dir_all(parent)
   136	                .map_err(|e| Error::Io(format!("creating {}: {e}", parent.display())))?;
   137	        }
   138	    }
   139	
   140	    ZstdBackend::new().diff(req.previous_installer, req.new_installer, req.patch_out)?;
   141	
   142	    let installer_digest = FileHash::of_file(req.new_installer)?;
   143	    let installer_size = file_size(req.new_installer)?;
   144	    let patch_digest = FileHash::of_file(req.patch_out)?;
   145	    let patch_size = file_size(req.patch_out)?;
   146	
   147	    // Over the target installer, not the patch: both the delta path and the
   148	    // full-download path end up holding this exact artifact, so one signature
   149	    // covers both.
   150	    let signature = key.sign_file(req.new_installer)?;
   151	
   152	    let patch = Patch {
   153	        backend_id: ZstdBackend::ID.to_owned(),
   154	        patch_url: req.patch_url.to_owned(),
   155	        patch_blake3: patch_digest.to_hex(),
   156	        patch_size,
   157	    };
   158	
   159	    let mut manifest = match existing {
   160	        Some(existing) if existing.version == req.version => existing,
   161	        _ => Manifest {
   162	            version: req.version.to_owned(),
   163	            notes: None,
   164	            pub_date: None,
   165	            platforms: Default::default(),
   166	            delta: None,
   167	        },
   168	    };
   169	
   170	    if let Some(notes) = req.notes {
   171	        manifest.notes = Some(notes.to_owned());
   172	    }
   173	    if let Some(pub_date) = req.pub_date {
   174	        manifest.pub_date = Some(pub_date.to_owned());
   175	    }
   176	
   177	    manifest.platforms.insert(
   178	        req.platform.to_owned(),
   179	        TauriPlatform {
   180	            url: req.installer_url.to_owned(),
   181	            signature: signature.clone(),
   182	        },
   183	    );
   184	
   185	    let delta = manifest.delta.get_or_insert_with(|| DeltaLayer {
   186	        schema: SCHEMA_VERSION,
   187	        hash_algo: HASH_ALGO.to_owned(),
   188	        platforms: Default::default(),
   189	    });
   190	
   191	    let entry = delta
   192	        .platforms
   193	        .entry(req.platform.to_owned())
   194	        .or_insert_with(|| DeltaPlatform {
   195	            target_version: req.version.to_owned(),
   196	            target_installer_blake3: installer_digest.to_hex(),
   197	            target_installer_size: installer_size,
   198	            signature: signature.clone(),
   199	            patches: Default::default(),
   200	        });
   201	
   202	    // Re-signing produces a different signature each run (minisign includes
   203	    // randomness), so keep the entry and the Tauri layer in step explicitly
   204	    // rather than relying on them having been written together.
   205	    entry.target_version = req.version.to_owned();
   206	    entry.target_installer_blake3 = installer_digest.to_hex();
   207	    entry.target_installer_size = installer_size;
   208	    entry.signature = signature;
   209	    entry.patches.insert(req.from_version.to_owned(), patch);
   210	
   211	    manifest.validate()?;
   212	
   213	    Ok((
   214	        manifest,
   215	        PatchSummary {
   216	            patch_size,
   217	            installer_size,
   218	        },
   219	    ))
   220	}

   224	        .map_err(|e| Error::Io(format!("stat {}: {e}", path.display())))?
   225	        .len())
   226	}

   230	/// A missing file is not an error — that is simply the first release.
   231	pub fn load_manifest(path: &Path) -> Result<Option<Manifest>> {
   232	    match std::fs::read_to_string(path) {

   234	        Err(e) if e.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound => Ok(None),

   239	/// Write a manifest to disk as pretty JSON.
   240	pub fn write_manifest(path: &Path, manifest: &Manifest) -> Result<()> {
   241	    let json = manifest.to_json()?;

   249	}

     2	//!
     3	//! File in, file out. Nothing here talks to the network, so it can be run
     4	//! locally against two installers exactly as CI runs it against two release
     5	//! artifacts.
     6	
     7	use std::path::PathBuf;

   136	/// Resolve the signing key from `--private-key` or the Tauri environment
   137	/// variables, accepting either an inline key or a path to one.
   138	fn load_key(explicit: Option<&str>) -> Result<SigningKey> {
   139	    let password = std::env::var(KEY_PASSWORD_ENV).ok();
   140	
   141	    let source = match explicit {
   142	        Some(value) => value.to_owned(),
   143	        None => std::env::var(KEY_ENV).map_err(|_| {
   144	            tauri_updater_delta_release::Error::Key(format!(
   145	                "no signing key: pass --private-key or set {KEY_ENV}"
   146	            ))
   147	        })?,
   148	    };
   149	
   150	    let path = PathBuf::from(&source);
   151	    if path.is_file() {
   152	        SigningKey::from_file(&path, password)
   153	    } else {
   154	        SigningKey::from_str(&source, password)
   155	    }
   156	}
     1	//! Minisign signing, in the shape Tauri's updater expects.
     2	//!
     3	//! Tauri stores signatures and keys as **base64 of the whole minisign file** —
     4	//! comment lines included — rather than as the raw signature bytes. Anything
     5	//! this tool writes into a manifest therefore has to go through the same
     6	//! encoding, or the official updater will reject it.
     7	//!
     8	//! Signing is prehashed (minisign's `ED` algorithm: Ed25519 over a BLAKE2b
     9	//! digest). That is what the `minisign` crate produces and what Tauri's own
    10	//! signer produces, and `minisign-verify` — the crate Tauri verifies with —
    11	//! accepts it.
    12	
    13	use std::path::Path;
    14	
    15	use base64::Engine as _;
    16	use minisign::{PublicKeyBox, SecretKey, SecretKeyBox};
    17	
    18	use crate::{Error, Result};
    19	
    20	/// A minisign secret key, ready to sign release artifacts.
    21	pub struct SigningKey {
    22	    secret: SecretKey,
    23	}
    24	
    25	impl SigningKey {
    26	    /// Load a key from the text form Tauri uses.
    27	    ///
    28	    /// Accepts either the raw minisign secret key file, or that file base64
    29	    /// encoded, which is what `tauri signer generate` prints and what people
    30	    /// paste into `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`. Trying raw first and base64
    31	    /// second means both work without the caller having to say which it has.
    32	    ///
    33	    /// `password` of `None` means **the key is unencrypted** — not "ask the
    34	    /// user". The `minisign` crate treats `None` as a request to prompt on the
    35	    /// terminal, which in CI has no TTY: the run dies with
    36	    /// `Device not configured (os error 6)`, or worse, hangs waiting for input
    37	    /// that will never come. A release tool must never do either, so `None` is
    38	    /// translated to an empty password here.
    39	    pub fn from_str(text: &str, password: Option<String>) -> Result<Self> {
    40	        let text = normalize_key_text(text, "secret key")?;
    41	
    42	        let boxed = SecretKeyBox::from_string(&text)
    43	            .map_err(|e| Error::Key(format!("unusable secret key: {e}")))?;
    44	
    45	        // Always Some(_), never None — see the note on this function.
    46	        let had_password = password.as_deref().is_some_and(|p| !p.is_empty());
    47	        let secret = boxed
    48	            .into_secret_key(Some(password.unwrap_or_default()))
    49	            .map_err(|e| {
    50	                // Tauri's CLI signs with rsign2, which runs its KDF even over an
    51	                // empty password. The `minisign` crate skips encryption entirely
    52	                // when the password is empty, so a key generated by
    53	                // `tauri signer generate --password ""` cannot be opened here at
    54	                // all — with any password. Say so, rather than leaving the user
    55	                // staring at "wrong password" for a key that has none.
    56	                if !had_password {
    57	                    Error::Key(format!(
    58	                        "could not unlock the secret key: {e}. If this key was made by \
    59	                         `tauri signer generate` with an empty password, it cannot be read \
    60	                         here: Tauri uses rsign2, which encrypts even with an empty \
    61	                         password, while this tool uses the minisign crate, which does not. \
    62	                         Regenerate the key with a real password and set \
    63	                         TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD."
    64	                    ))
    65	                } else {
    66	                    Error::Key(format!("could not unlock the secret key: {e}"))
    67	                }
    68	            })?;
    69	
    70	        Ok(Self { secret })
    71	    }
    72	
    73	    /// Load a key from a file on disk.
    74	    pub fn from_file(path: &Path, password: Option<String>) -> Result<Self> {
    75	        let text = std::fs::read_to_string(path)
    76	            .map_err(|e| Error::Io(format!("reading key {}: {e}", path.display())))?;
    77	        Self::from_str(&text, password)
    78	    }
    79	
    80	    /// Sign a file, returning the base64 form Tauri stores in its manifest.
    81	    ///
    82	    /// The signature is over the artifact's bytes, so it stays valid however the
    83	    /// artifact reached the user — downloaded whole, or rebuilt from a patch.
    84	    pub fn sign_file(&self, path: &Path) -> Result<String> {
    85	        let file = std::fs::File::open(path)
    86	            .map_err(|e| Error::Io(format!("opening {} to sign: {e}", path.display())))?;
    87	
    88	        let signature = minisign::sign(None, &self.secret, file, None, None)
    89	            .map_err(|e| Error::Sign(format!("signing {}: {e}", path.display())))?;
    90	
    91	        Ok(base64::engine::general_purpose::STANDARD.encode(signature.into_string()))
    92	    }
    93	}

    95	/// Decode a Tauri-style base64 public key into its raw minisign form.
    96	///
    97	/// Useful for verifying what this tool produced without shelling out.
    98	pub fn decode_public_key(text: &str) -> Result<minisign::PublicKey> {
    99	    let text = normalize_key_text(text, "public key")?;
   100	    PublicKeyBox::from_string(&text)
   101	        .map_err(|e| Error::Key(format!("unusable public key: {e}")))?
   102	        .into_public_key()
   103	        .map_err(|e| Error::Key(format!("unusable public key: {e}")))
   104	}
   105	
   106	/// Minisign key and signature files all begin with this line.
   107	const COMMENT_PREFIX: &str = "untrusted comment:";
   108	
   109	/// Return the raw minisign file text, decoding the base64 wrapper if present.
   110	///
   111	/// This has to branch on *content*, not on whether parsing succeeds:
   112	/// `SecretKeyBox::from_string` and `PublicKeyBox::from_string` accept any string
   113	/// at all and only fail later, when the key is used. A "try raw, fall back to
   114	/// base64" approach therefore never reaches the fallback, and a base64 key fails
   115	/// much later with a confusing "Missing encoded key" instead.
   116	fn normalize_key_text(text: &str, what: &str) -> Result<String> {
   117	    let trimmed = text.trim();
   118	    if trimmed.starts_with(COMMENT_PREFIX) {
   119	        return Ok(trimmed.to_owned());
   120	    }
   121	
   122	    // Tauri stores keys base64-encoded; some tools wrap that at column 64.
   123	    let compact: String = trimmed.chars().filter(|c| !c.is_whitespace()).collect();
   124	    let decoded = base64::engine::general_purpose::STANDARD
   125	        .decode(&compact)
   126	        .map_err(|_| Error::Key(format!("{what} is neither minisign text nor base64")))?;
   127	    let decoded = String::from_utf8(decoded)
   128	        .map_err(|_| Error::Key(format!("{what} base64 did not decode to text")))?;
   129

     2	//!
     3	//! The whole module sits behind `#[cfg(feature = "e2e-control")]` at its
     4	//! declaration in `main.rs`, and the feature is not in `default`. With the
     5	//! feature off there is no listener, no port, and no code — not a disabled
     6	//! branch, but nothing at all in the binary.
     7	//!
     8	//! That is verified rather than asserted: the harness builds the app without
     9	//! the feature and checks both that the marker string is absent from the binary
    10	//! and that nothing is listening. A test-only HTTP surface that ships is a
    11	//! vulnerability added deliberately and then forgotten, so "we remembered to
    12	//! gate it" is not a good enough standard.
    13	//!
    14	//! # Why this exists at all
    15	//!
    16	//! `tauri_plugin_updater::Update` has private fields, so no test can construct
    17	//! one; only `Updater::check()` inside a running app can. Driving the app from
    18	//! outside therefore requires *some* control channel, and the alternatives —
    19	//! AppleScript, accessibility APIs, synthetic UI events — are more fragile,
    20	//! more platform-specific and harder to reason about than a loopback socket.
    21	//!
    22	//! # Shape
    23	//!
    24	//! Plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1, one thread, no dependencies:
    25	//!
    26	//! - `GET /trigger` — run one update, block until it finishes, return the outcome.
    27	//! - `GET /outcome` — the last outcome, or `none`.
    28	//! - `GET /version` — the running app's version.
    29	
    30	use std::io::{BufRead, BufReader, Write};
    31	use std::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream};
    32	use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
    33	
    34	use tauri::{AppHandle, Runtime};
    35	
    36	/// Grep target for the "did this ship?" check. Deliberately distinctive.
    37	const CONTROL_MARKER: &str = "DELTA_E2E_CONTROL_SURFACE_PRESENT";
    38	
    39	/// Start the control surface on the port in `DELTA_E2E_CONTROL_PORT`.
    40	///
    41	/// Writes the bound port to `DELTA_E2E_CONTROL_PORT_FILE` if set, so the
    42	/// harness can use port 0 and discover it.
    43	pub fn spawn<R: Runtime>(app: AppHandle<R>) {
    44	    let port: u16 = std::env::var("DELTA_E2E_CONTROL_PORT")
    45	        .ok()
    46	        .and_then(|p| p.parse().ok())
    47	        .unwrap_or(0);
    48	
    49	    let listener = match TcpListener::bind(("127.0.0.1", port)) {
    50	        Ok(listener) => listener,
    51	        Err(e) => {
    52	            eprintln!("{CONTROL_MARKER}: could not bind: {e}");
    53	            return;
    54	        }
    55	    };
    56	
    57	    if let Ok(addr) = listener.local_addr() {
    58	        eprintln!("{CONTROL_MARKER}: listening on {addr}");
    59	        if let Ok(path) = std::env::var("DELTA_E2E_CONTROL_PORT_FILE") {
    60	            let _ = std::fs::write(path, addr.port().to_string());
    61	        }
    62	    }
    63	
    64	    let last_outcome = Arc::new(Mutex::new(String::from("none")));
    65	
    66	    std::thread::spawn(move || {
    67	        for stream in listener.incoming().flatten() {
    68	            let app = app.clone();
    69	            let last_outcome = Arc::clone(&last_outcome);
    70	            // Serially, not per-connection threads: an update mutates the app
    71	            // bundle, and two at once would be meaningless.
    72	            if let Err(e) = handle(stream, &app, &last_outcome) {
    73	                eprintln!("{CONTROL_MARKER}: request failed: {e}");
    74	            }
    75	        }
    76	    });
    77	}
    78	
    79	fn handle<R: Runtime>(
    80	    mut stream: TcpStream,
    81	    app: &AppHandle<R>,
    82	    last_outcome: &Mutex<String>,
    83	) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    84	    let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream.try_clone()?);
    85	    let mut request_line = String::new();
    86	    reader.read_line(&mut request_line)?;
    87	    loop {
    88	        let mut line = String::new();
    89	        if reader.read_line(&mut line)? == 0 || line == "\r\n" || line == "\n" {
    90	            break;
    91	        }
    92	    }
    93	
    94	    let path = request_line.split_whitespace().nth(1).unwrap_or("/");
    95	
    96	    let body = match path {
    97	        "/trigger" => {
    98	            let result = crate::update::run(app);
    99	            let text = match result {
   100	                Ok(outcome) => format!("ok {outcome}"),
   101	                // Reported, not swallowed: the harness asserts on loud failures
   102	                // too, notably the signature case in DECISIONS #11.
   103	                Err(e) => format!("error {e}"),
   104	            };
   105	            *last_outcome.lock().expect("outcome lock") = text.clone();
   106	            text
   107	        }
   108	        "/outcome" => last_outcome.lock().expect("outcome lock").clone(),
   109	        "/version" => app.package_info().version.to_string(),
   110	        _ => "unknown".to_owned(),
   111	    };
   112	
   113	    write!(
   114	        stream,
   115	        "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/plain\r\nContent-Length: {}\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n{body}",
   116	        body.len()
   117	    )?;
   118	    stream.flush()
   119	}

# Sprint 4 — The real-app end-to-end

**Phase:** 3 of 8, final gate ([roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md))
**Started:** 2026-08-12
**Status:** In progress

## Goal

Close the one claim still open: **a running Tauri app accepts a served update.**

Everything to date proves the algorithm. Nothing proves that a real
`Update`, obtained from a real `Updater::check()` inside a real app, installs a
delta-rebuilt artifact. 103 tests use a fake handoff — by design, and that is
exactly why none of them substitutes for this.

## Why an app is unavoidable

`tauri_plugin_updater::Update` has private fields (`run_on_main_thread`,
`config`, `extract_path`, `app_name`, `installer_args`). No test can construct
one. `Updater::check()` inside a running app is the only source, so the
control-surface route is **forced, not chosen**.

The counterweight: macOS `install_inner` is pure file manipulation — gzip, tar
extract, rename the live bundle, move the new one in. No GUI surface, so once a
real `Update` exists the install is mechanical and hash-assertable.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Two versions built by `cargo tauri build`, published through `delta-release`
- [ ] Local plain-HTTP server, no cloud, no external dependencies
- [ ] Post-install BLAKE3 of the **main binary** matches v_new, by name, by hash
- [ ] Failure branches asserted by outcome, not by error
- [ ] DECISIONS #13 recording the Gatekeeper path taken and what it proves
- [ ] SPRINT / CHANGELOG / docs updated in the same PR

## Tasks

### 1. Example app — done

- [x] `examples/desktop-app`, Tauri v2, plain HTML frontend, no npm build step
- [x] Registers both plugins; real "check for updates" action in the UI
- [x] The update path is the genuine integration: Tauri's own `check()` reads
      the manifest (works because it is a *superset*, decision #5), yielding the
      `Update` that installs; our flow substitutes only the download

### 2. Control surface — done, and verified absent by default

- [x] `#[cfg(feature = "e2e-control")]`, feature **not** in `default`
- [x] Loopback HTTP only: `/trigger`, `/outcome`, `/version`
- [x] Triggers the *same* function the UI button calls, so tested path and
      shipped path are the same code
- [x] **Verified by evidence, not inspection:** default build has no marker
      string in the binary; the check is non-vacuous because the marker *is*
      present when the feature is explicitly enabled

No private key is committed either — the harness generates one per run. A
test-only key in the repo is the same hazard class as a shipped test surface.

### 3. Two published versions — in progress

- [ ] `cargo tauri build` producing `.app` and `.app.tar.gz`
- [ ] v_old and v_new differing in the **main binary**, not just metadata
- [ ] Both published through `delta-release`, not hand-crafted

### 4. Harness

- [ ] Serve manifest + patch + `.app.tar.gz` over the existing `TestServer`
- [ ] Assert v_old != v_new **at the main-binary layer** — different metadata
      around an identical binary is the `appimage_pair` vacuous pass arriving
      through a different door

### 5. The install

- [ ] Direct route: ad-hoc codesign, `xattr -cr`, run `Update::install` on the
      live bundle
- [ ] Assert the installed bundle's main binary hashes to v_new
- [ ] If `PermissionDenied` or an authorization prompt blocks a headless run,
      take the stripped-down fallback and record it — do not paper over it

### 6. Failure branches

- [ ] corrupt / truncated / wrong-base patch → fallback → installed bytes are
      the released artifact
- [ ] signature failure → no install, loud failure, per DECISIONS #11
- [ ] corrupt full download → nothing installed

Building the two app versions.

## Blocked

Nothing.

## Notes

- Claim status: **"a running Tauri app accepts a served update" is OPEN.** It
  closes only if the direct install path succeeds. The stripped-down fallback
  closes a weaker claim and leaves the full one open, recorded as such.
- Base-artifact caching is not built; the harness supplies the previous
  artifact directly. A shipping plugin would cache it after each update. That
  gap is real and belongs to Phase 3 proper.

## Next sprint

Phase 4 — robustness: resumable downloads, disk-full, atomic writes, and an
audit of every failure branch. Much of it already exists; the work is closing
gaps rather than starting fresh.
# Test signing keys

**No private key lives here, and none should.**

`e2e-test.key.pub` is a placeholder public key so the example app's
`tauri.conf.json` is coherent when built by hand. Nobody holds the matching
private key — it was generated and discarded.

The end-to-end harness generates a **fresh keypair per run** into a temporary
directory, writes the public half into `tauri.conf.json` before building, and
signs the release artifacts with the private half. Nothing secret is ever
written into the repository.

This is deliberate. A test-only private key committed "because it signs nothing
real" is the same class of hazard as a test-only HTTP surface that ships: safe
by intent, dangerous by accident, and impossible to notice once it is old. Not
committing it makes the hazard structurally absent rather than documented.

   106	## 5. The manifest is a superset of Tauri's, not a second document
   107	
   108	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active
   109	
   110	`manifest.json` carries Tauri's own `version`, `notes`, `pub_date` and
   111	`platforms` fields untouched, with the delta information under a separate
   112	`delta` key.
   113	
   114	The alternative — publishing a delta manifest next to Tauri's — means two
   115	documents that must agree about URLs, versions and signatures, updated by
   116	different code paths. They *will* drift, and the failure mode is the worst one
   117	available: a client that falls back to a full download and finds the fallback
   118	description stale.
   119	
   120	Making one document serve both readers removes the possibility. A delta-unaware
   121	Tauri client reads this file and behaves exactly as it does today; the delta path
   122	is additive. `the_published_manifest_is_a_valid_tauri_document` asserts that
   123	property directly against the JSON the tool writes.
   124	
   125	**Revisit when:** Tauri's static manifest format changes shape.

   129	## 6. The signature covers the target installer, not the patch
   130	
   131	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active
   132	
   133	The minisign signature in both layers is over the **installer that gets
   134	installed** — never over the patch.
   135	
   136	Both paths converge on the same artifact: a full download fetches it, the delta
   137	path rebuilds it. Signing that artifact means one signature validates both, and
   138	the delta path is incapable of installing anything the full-download path would
   139	have rejected. Signing the *patch* instead would establish only that the patch
   140	was authentic, which says nothing about what it produced.
   141	
   142	**Constraints this imposes:**
   143	
   144	- **Every published delta requires the release signing key.** There is no way to
   145	  produce a valid manifest entry without it, and CI fails loudly rather than
   146	  emitting an unsigned manifest.
   147	- **Signing happens after the artifact is final.** The signature covers exact
   148	  bytes, so anything that rewrites the installer afterwards — re-compression, a
   149	  notarization staple — invalidates it and must run before this tool.
   150	- **Re-signing is not idempotent.** Minisign includes randomness, so signing the
   151	  same file twice yields different strings. Both layers are therefore written
   152	  from a single signing operation per run, and `Manifest::validate` rejects a
   153	  document where they disagree.
   154	**Validated against Tauri's actual verifier** (2026-08-12, the first task of
   155	Phase 3, before any client flow was built on top of it).
   156	
   157	`crates/delta-release/tests/tauri_signature_compat.rs` reproduces
   158	`tauri-plugin-updater` 2.10.1's `verify_signature` and `base64_to_string`
   159	**verbatim** — copied, not paraphrased — and runs them against signatures
   160	`delta-release` actually produces. Paraphrasing would have hidden a real
   161	difference: Tauri calls `PublicKey::decode` on the whole base64-decoded key
   162	file, not `from_base64` on the key line, and a check written from memory would
   163	plausibly get that wrong and still pass.

   165	Findings:
   166	
   167	- Tauri accepts the signature in **both** manifest layers.
   168	- The signature is **prehashed** (`ED`, bytes `0x45 0x44`), asserted two
   169	  independent ways: directly on the wire format, and by verifying with
   170	  `allow_legacy = false`, which rejects any non-prehashed signature outright —
   171	  so success there can only mean the prehashed branch ran. This matters because
   172	  Tauri passes `allow_legacy = true`, meaning a merely-green verification would
   173	  not have told us which code path executed.
   174	- In `minisign-verify`, `verify` branches on `signature.is_prehashed` *before*

   176	- Tauri rejects a signature over different bytes, and one from another key.
   177	- **An artifact rebuilt from a delta satisfies the same signature a full
   178	  download would have been checked against** — which is the entire point of
   179	  signing the target installer.

   181	Version alignment: Tauri pins `minisign-verify = "0.2"` and so does this

   187	separate claims.

   191	## 7. Schema 1 patches only to the latest release
   192	
   193	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active
   194	
   195	Every entry in a platform's `patches` map reconstructs the *current* release
   196	directly. A user on any listed previous version applies exactly one patch.
   197	
   198	Multi-hop chaining — 1.0.0 → 1.0.1 → 1.0.2 — would let a release publish one
   199	small patch instead of one per supported previous version. It also means a client
   200	applying several patches in sequence, where an intermediate result must be
   201	verified before it can be used as the next base, and a single missing link
   202	strands everyone downstream of it. Not worth it before there is evidence that
   203	publishing N patches per release is a real cost.
   204	
   205	Because of this, publishing a new version *replaces* the delta layer rather than
   206	merging into it: entries that rebuild the previous release are stale the moment a
   207	newer one ships. `a_new_release_replaces_patches_that_target_the_old_one` pins
   208	that behaviour.
   209	
   210	**Revisit when:** the number of supported upgrade paths makes per-release patch
   211	generation expensive. Chaining would ship as `schema: 2`, and the `schema` field
   212	exists so an older client refuses it cleanly instead of misreading it.
   213	
   214	---

   216	## 8. The window bound is enforced now, not deferred to Phase 4
   217	
   218	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active
   219	
   220	Phase 1 left a gap: `apply` bounded the bytes it wrote, but not the window zstd
   221	was allowed to allocate. A patch whose frame header declared a large window log
   222	could force an allocation of up to 2 GiB before anything was validated.
   223	
   224	The manifest now states the target installer's exact size, so the fix is
   225	available immediately and is a few lines — derive the window log from
   226	`max(base size, declared size)` instead of permitting zstd's maximum. Deferring
   227	it to Phase 4 would have meant shipping a known allocation vector through an
   228	entire phase for no benefit, so it is closed here.
   229	
   230	The declared size doubles as a correctness gate: a patch that decompresses
   231	cleanly to the wrong length now fails with `UnexpectedOutputSize` before the
   232	digest is even computed.
   233	
   234	**Note:** this bounds allocation for patches applied *through a manifest*. The
   235	backend still accepts an unbounded call for use without one, which is what the
   236	release tool and the Phase 1 round-trip tests use. Client code always goes
   237	through `try_reconstruct`, which always supplies the size.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## 9. `try_reconstruct` cannot fail
   242	
   243	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active
   244	
   245	The delta path's entry point returns a `Reconstruction`, not a `Result`. Its two
   246	variants are "here is a verified artifact" and "download the full one".
   247	
   248	The safety property — a bad patch can never break an install — is otherwise
   249	enforced only by every caller remembering to catch every error. Making the
   250	function infallible moves that from convention into the type system: there is no
   251	error value that can escape the delta path and abort an update.
   252	
   253	---
   254	
   255	## 10. The plugin must verify the signature itself — Tauri will not
   256	
   257	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active · **Corrects an earlier assumption**
   258	
   259	The original design said the reconstructed artifact "still has to satisfy Tauri's
   260	minisign verification". Reading `tauri-plugin-updater` 2.10.1 while building the
   261	handoff showed that is false, and it matters enough to record rather than quietly
   262	fix.
   263	
   264	`verify_signature` is called from **exactly one place** in the whole crate:
   265	
   266	```rust
   267	// src/updater.rs:712, inside Update::download()
   268	verify_signature(&buffer, &self.signature, &self.config.pubkey)?;
   269	```
   270	
   271	The handoff seam goes nowhere near it:
   272	
   273	```rust
   274	// src/updater.rs:718
   275	pub fn install(&self, bytes: impl AsRef<[u8]>) -> Result<()> {
   276	    self.install_inner(bytes.as_ref())   // no verification
   277	}
   278	```
   279	
   280	`download_and_install` is just `download()` then `install()`, so verification
   281	belongs to the download step. The delta path exists precisely to avoid that
   282	download — so **nothing verifies the signature unless this plugin does**.
   283	
   284	The design survives; the reasoning had a hole. The plugin performs the check
   285	itself before every handoff, using Tauri's verification reproduced verbatim and
   286	pinned by `crates/delta-release/tests/tauri_signature_compat.rs`.
   287	
   288	This promotes that compatibility gate from reassuring to load-bearing. It is no
   289	longer "evidence we interoperate" — it is the only thing standing between a
   290	reconstructed artifact and the installer. Any change to it needs the same rigour
   291	as a change to the verification itself.
   292	
   293	**Had this gone unnoticed**, the delta path would have become a way to install
   294	artifacts with no signature check at all — the exact outcome the wrap-don't-
   295	replace design exists to prevent, arrived at while believing the opposite.
   296	
   297	**Revisit when:** upstream moves verification into `install`, or exposes a
   298	verifying handoff. Then this becomes redundant and should be deleted rather than
   299	left to rot alongside a second implementation.
   300	
   301	---
   302	
   303	## 11. Everything falls back except a signature failure
   304	
   305	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active
   306	
   307	The delta path falls back to a full download on every failure — corrupt patch,
   308	truncated patch, transport error, wrong base version, unknown backend, digest
   309	mismatch, out of disk. **One case does not: a signature failure aborts.**
   310	
   311	The precise rule is not "delta failures fall back". It is:
   312	
   313	> Fall back on any failure that does not call the *manifest's authenticity* into
   314	> question. A signature failure is the sole case where the manifest itself is
   315	> under suspicion, so no fallback path exists.
   316	
   317	Everything else is a statement about one artifact or one transfer, and says
   318	nothing about whether the release document is genuine. A signature failure says
   319	the opposite.
   320	
   321	### Why there is nothing to fall back to
   322	
   323	This follows directly from decision #5, the manifest-as-superset. The
   324	full-download URL and the delta information live in **one document**, covered by
   325	**one signature over the target installer**. So if that signature does not check
   326	out, the document is untrustworthy in its entirety — including the
   327	`platforms.<target>.url` a fallback would fetch from.
   328	
   329	Falling back would download an artifact chosen by a document we have just decided
   330	we cannot trust, and would then verify it against a signature from that same
   331	document. It preserves the risk while presenting itself as the safe option, which
   332	is worse than failing loudly: the user believes a safety mechanism engaged when
   333	it did not.
   334	
   335	### The load-bearing condition
   336	
   337	**This reasoning depends on the full-artifact URL and hash sharing one signed
   338	document with the delta information.** That is true of schema 1 and is a
   339	consequence of #5.
   340	
   341	If a future change ever splits them — a Tauri-native manifest plus a separate
   342	delta sidecar, signed independently — **this asymmetry must be re-examined**. In
   343	that world a delta-side signature failure would say nothing about the
   344	Tauri-native document, and falling back could be both safe and correct. The
   345	conclusion would change even though the code would still compile and every test
   346	would still pass.
   347	
   348	Not a change being made. Recorded so a later refactor cannot quietly reopen the
   349	question by moving the ground the argument stands on.
   350	
   351	---
   352	
   353	## 12. MSRV moves to 1.88 when `tauri` enters the workspace
   354	
   355	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active · **Supersedes the floor in #4**
   356	
   357	Adding `tauri` raised the minimum from 1.85 to **1.88**. CI caught it: the `msrv`
   358	job went red on the branch that introduced the dependency, while all three test
   359	jobs stayed green.

   362	| --- | --- |
   363	| `darling` 0.23.0 (and `_core`, `_macro`) | rustc 1.88.0 |
   364	| `icu_collections`, `icu_locale_core` 2.2.0 | rustc 1.86 |
   365

   368	
   369	Worth recording as a *design* note rather than a version bump: this is the price
   370	of the wrap-don't-replace decision. Depending on `tauri` means inheriting its
   371	whole dependency tree's floor, and that floor will keep moving. The engine
   372	crates would still build on 1.85 — only the plugin needs 1.88 — so if a low MSRV
   373	ever matters more than a single workspace-wide number, the split already exists
   374	along the right seam.
   375

   378	after release, which is the whole reason the job exists.

   382	## 13. Delta is correctness-only on macOS until the tar layer is addressed
   383	
   384	**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active, tracked as Phase 4/5 work
   385	
   386	Measured on the real example app, two versions built by `cargo tauri build` and
   387	published by `delta-release`:
   388	
   389	| Platform | Artifact | Patch | Full | Patch as % of download |
   390	| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
   391	| Linux | `.AppImage` (synthetic fixture) | 393,782 | 6,815,744 | **5.78%** |
   392	| macOS | `.app.tar.gz` (real bundle) | 3,860,122 | 4,057,308 | **95.14%** |

    65	Four stages, in order:
    66	
    67	1. **Diff** happens at release time, on CI, not on the user's machine. For each
    68	   supported upgrade path (`1.2.0 → 1.3.0`, `1.2.1 → 1.3.0`, …) the release
    69	   tooling produces a patch and records its size and the resulting artifact hash
    70	   in a patch manifest.
    71	2. **Apply** happens on the client: base artifact + patch → rebuilt artifact.
    72	3. **Verify** hashes the rebuilt artifact and compares it against the hash in the
    73	   manifest. This catches a corrupt patch, a corrupt base, a wrong base version
    74	   and a bug in the backend, all with one check.
    75	4. **Handoff** passes the verified file to the platform adapter, which gives it
    76	   to the official updater's install step.
    77	
    78	### Where the base artifact comes from
    79	
    80	Applying a patch requires the *old* artifact, and an installed app does not
    81	normally keep the installer it came from. Two strategies, both planned:
    82	
    83	- **Cache the artifact** after an update completes, so the next update has its
    84	  base ready. Cheap, but useless for the very first delta update and for anyone
    85	  who installed from the website.
    86	- **Reconstruct the base** from what is on disk where the installed layout allows
    87	  it deterministically.
    88	
    89	Until a base is available, the plugin simply does a full download. The design
    90	never assumes the base is present.
    91	
    92	## The `PatchBackend` trait
    93	
    94	Delta algorithms have genuinely different trade-offs — patch size against memory
    95	use against apply speed — and the right one depends on the artifact. The engine
    96	is written against a trait so a backend can be swapped without touching the rest
    97	of the pipeline:
    98	
    99	```rust
   100	pub trait PatchBackend: Send + Sync {
   101	    /// Stable identifier recorded in the patch manifest, e.g. "zstd".
   102	    fn id(&self) -> &'static str;
   103	
   104	    /// Release-side: produce a patch that turns `old` into `new`.
   105	    fn diff(&self, old: &Path, new: &Path, patch: &Path) -> Result<()>;
   106	
   107	    /// Client-side: reconstruct `new` from `old` + `patch`.
   108	    fn apply(&self, old: &Path, patch: &Path, out: &Path) -> Result<()>;
   109	}
   110	```
   111	
   112	The manifest records which backend produced each patch, so a client can decline
   113	a patch it cannot apply (and fall back) rather than guessing. That makes adding
   114	a backend a backwards-compatible change.
   115	
   116	**Backend 1 — zstd `--patch-from`.** The old artifact is referenced as a
   117	compression *prefix*, with the window log raised to cover its full size, so the
   118	compressor can copy directly from it. Mature, widely deployed, one dependency,
   119	and fast to apply. This is the default.
   120	
   121	**Backend 2 — bsdiff (planned).** Produces materially smaller patches for
   122	recompiled binaries because it tolerates the small shifts a recompile causes, at
   123	the cost of much higher memory use during diff. A candidate for release-time use
   124	where CI memory is cheap.
   125	
   126	## Per-platform adapter seams
   127	
   128	Everything above is shared. Per-platform code is confined to one small trait: how
   129	to obtain the base artifact, and how to hand the rebuilt one to the installer.
   130	
   131	| Platform | Artifact | Notes |
   132	| --- | --- | --- |
   133	| Linux | `.AppImage` | Simplest case: a single self-contained file, no installer step, no code signature to preserve. This is why it is the first target — and why the engine can be proven on macOS, since round-tripping an AppImage is just file I/O. |
   134	| Windows | NSIS `.exe` / `.msi` | Artifact is a single file. Handoff means pointing the existing installer-launch step at the rebuilt file. |
   135	| macOS | `.app.tar.gz` | Compressed tarball, so unrelated changes perturb the compressed stream widely. Likely needs the delta taken against the *uncompressed* tar and the gzip layer reproduced deterministically — the hardest of the three, hence last. |
   136	
   137	## Failure model
   138	
   139	The safety property is: **the delta path can only ever make an update faster,
   140	never make it fail.**
   141	
   142	Every step from manifest lookup to hash verification is fallible and every
   143	failure has exactly one recovery: discard whatever the delta path produced and
   144	let the official updater do a full download. There is no error state in which the
   145	user is left worse off than if this plugin were not installed.
   146	
   147	`delta_core::Error` is `#[non_exhaustive]` and every variant is treated as
   148	recoverable at the plugin boundary. Nothing in the delta path panics on
   149	malformed or hostile input.
   150	
   151	## Security notes
   152	
   153	- **The hash check is a correctness gate, not the trust anchor.** Authenticity
   154	  comes from the minisign signature over the target installer. A patch is
   155	  untrusted input; it is only ever used to produce a candidate file that must
   156	  then pass both checks.
   157	- **The plugin performs the signature check itself, and must.** This was
   158	  originally written assuming Tauri would verify whatever it was handed. It does
   159	  not. In `tauri-plugin-updater` 2.10.1, `verify_signature` is called from
   160	  exactly one place — inside `Update::download()` — and the handoff seam,
   161	  `Update::install(bytes)`, goes straight to the installer with no verification.
   162	  Since the delta path exists precisely to avoid `download()`, nothing would
   163	  check the signature unless the plugin does. It therefore runs the check before
   164	  every handoff, using Tauri's own verification code reproduced verbatim and
   165	  pinned by `tauri_signature_compat.rs`. Skipping it would turn the delta path
   166	  into a way to install unsigned artifacts, which is the one outcome this design
   167	  exists to prevent.
   168	- **Patches are treated as hostile.** Apply streams its output to disk and stops
   169	  at a configurable ceiling, so a malicious patch cannot expand indefinitely or
   170	  fill the user's disk.
   171	- **Allocation is bounded before decompression starts.** The manifest declares
   172	  the target installer's exact size, so the window zstd may allocate is derived
   173	  from a number the release committed to in advance rather than from the patch's
   174	  own header. A patch claiming a huge window log is rejected during frame setup.
   175	  This closed the gap Phase 1 documented here.
   176	- **No new network surface.** The plugin fetches from the update server the app
   177	  already configures, and sends no telemetry.
   178	
   179	## The manifest
   180	
   181	Release-time output is a single `manifest.json` that is **a superset of Tauri's
   182	own static updater document**. Tauri's `version`, `notes`, `pub_date` and
   183	`platforms` fields are present and untouched; delta information lives under a
   184	separate `delta` key.
   185	
   186	That shape is deliberate. Publishing a second, delta-specific document would mean
   187	two files that have to agree about URLs, versions and signatures while being
   188	written by different code paths — and the drift shows up exactly when it hurts
   189	most, in the fallback. One document cannot disagree with itself.
   190	
   191	```
   192	manifest.json
   193	├── version, notes, pub_date          ── read by every Tauri client
   194	├── platforms/<os-arch>/{url,signature}  ── the full-download fallback
   195	└── delta/
   196	    ├── schema, hash_algo
   197	    └── platforms/<os-arch>/
   198	        ├── target_version
   199	        ├── target_installer_blake3   ── the reconstruction gate
   200	        ├── target_installer_size     ── bounds allocation before decompressing
   201	        ├── signature                 ── same value as the Tauri layer
   202	        └── patches/<from_version>/{backend_id, patch_url, patch_blake3, patch_size}
   203	```
   204	
   205	Three properties worth stating explicitly:
   206	
   207	- **The signature is over the target installer, never the patch.** Both paths end
   208	  up holding the same artifact, so one signature validates both, and the delta
   209	  path cannot install anything the full-download path would have refused.
   210	- **Hashes name their algorithm.** Fields are `*_blake3` and `hash_algo` is
   211	  explicit, so a client refuses a document it cannot check rather than comparing
   212	  a BLAKE3 digest against a field that once held SHA-256.
   213	- **Schema 1 patches only to the latest release.** One patch per update, never a
   214	  chain. The `schema` field lets an older client decline a format it does not
   215	  implement instead of misreading it.
   216	
   217	## The release side
   218	
   219	`delta-release` is file-in, file-out: previous installer plus new installer
   220	produces the patch, the digests, the signature and the manifest. It runs on CI
   221	once per release, never on a user's machine, and needs no network access — which
   222	also makes it runnable by hand against two local files.
   223	
   224	Because the engine and the tooling are tested against the identical fixtures, the
   225	loop is closed in CI: a manifest generated by the real tool is handed to a
   226	simulated client with nothing else, and the client has to reach a verified
   227	artifact using only what the manifest recorded.
   228	
   229	## What this plugin deliberately does not do
   230	
   231	- Patch installed binaries in place.
   232	- Replace, fork or vendor `tauri-plugin-updater`.
   233	- Change how artifacts are signed, verified or installed.
   234	- Require a particular hosting setup — the patch manifest is a static JSON file
   235	  and can sit next to the existing update endpoint.
     1	# Roadmap
     2	
     3	Phases are ordered so that each one is provable before the next begins. The
     4	guiding constraint: development is happening on macOS with no Windows or Linux
     5	machine available, so early phases are chosen to be fully verifiable here.
     6	
     7	Platform order is **Linux (AppImage) → Windows → macOS end-to-end**, which is
     8	deliberately not the development machine's own platform. AppImage is a single
     9	self-contained file with no installer step and no code signature to preserve, so
    10	the diff/apply engine can be proven against it with nothing but file I/O — which
    11	runs anywhere, including here. macOS is last because `.app.tar.gz` is the hardest
    12	artifact to delta well.
    13	
    14	---
    15	
    16	## Phase 1 — The engine ✅
    17	
    18	Prove that a patch can rebuild an artifact exactly, on this machine, offline.
    19	
    20	- Workspace, project hygiene, docs, CI.
    21	- `PatchBackend` trait; zstd as backend #1.
    22	- Content hashing and verification.
    23	- **Flagship test:** AppImage-shaped round-trip — two versions of a file, diff,
    24	  apply, assert `hash(rebuilt) == hash(new)`. Must pass in CI.
    25	- First real patch-size numbers for the README.
    26	
    27	*Exit criteria:* round-trip test green in CI; patch measurably smaller than a full
    28	artifact; corrupt and mismatched inputs fail loudly rather than silently.
    29	
    30	*Delivered:* 6,815,744 byte artifact → 393,782 byte patch (5.78%), reproduced
    31	byte-identically on Linux, macOS and Windows and asserted in CI.
    32	
    33	## Phase 2 — Release tooling and CI ✅
    34	
    35	Make patches producible by a real release pipeline.
    36	
    37	- Patch manifest format (versions, backend id, patch URL, sizes, artifact hash).
    38	- CLI to generate patches and a manifest from a set of released artifacts.
    39	- Retention policy — how many previous versions get a patch path.
    40	- A reusable GitHub Actions workflow other projects can call.
    41	
    42	*Exit criteria:* a tagged release produces patches and a valid manifest without
    43	manual steps.
    44	
    45	*Delivered:* `delta-release` (patch + digests + signature + manifest),
    46	the Tauri-superset manifest, a dry-runnable `release.yml`, and an end-to-end test
    47	where a client reaches a verified artifact from the generated manifest alone.
    48	Wiring the workflow to real bundler output waits for the Phase 3 example app.
    49	
    50	## Phase 3 — Client happy path
    51	
    52	First end-to-end delta update, on Linux/AppImage.
    53	
    54	- Tauri plugin crate wrapping `tauri-plugin-updater`.
    55	- Manifest fetch, patch selection, download, apply, verify.
    56	- Base-artifact caching after a successful update.
    57	- Install handoff adapter for AppImage.
    58	- Example app demonstrating the update.
    59	
    60	*Exit criteria:* an AppImage app updates itself from a patch, verified in CI
    61	containers.
    62	
    63	## Phase 4 — Robustness and security
    64	
    65	Make it safe to depend on.
    66	
    67	- Full-download fallback wired into every failure path, with tests that force
    68	  each failure.
    69	- Bounded decompression; disk-space checks before writing.
    70	- Resume and retry for interrupted patch downloads.
    71	- Fuzzing the apply path against malformed patches.
    72	- Concurrency and interrupted-update handling.
    73	
    74	*Exit criteria:* every error variant has a test proving the update still
    75	completes via full download.
    76	
    77	## Phase 5 — Developer experience
    78	
    79	Make it pleasant to adopt.
    80	
    81	- TypeScript bindings and JS API.
    82	- Progress events distinguishing patch download from full download.
    83	- Configuration ergonomics and sensible defaults.
    84	- Documented migration from plain `tauri-plugin-updater` — ideally two lines.
    85	
    86	## Phase 6 — Windows
    87	
    88	- NSIS/MSI artifact handling and install handoff.
    89	- CI coverage on Windows runners.
    90	- Needs a real Windows tester.
    91	
    92	## Phase 7 — macOS end-to-end
    93	
    94	- `.app.tar.gz` handling, likely deltaing the uncompressed tar with
    95	  deterministic recompression.
    96	- Verify code signature and notarization survive intact.
    97	
    98	## Phase 8 — Ship
    99	
   100	- crates.io and npm publication.
   101	- Benchmarks across a few real-world app sizes.
   102	- Upstream: report back on tauri-apps/tauri#11863.
   103	
   104	---
   105	
   106	## Deliberately out of scope
   107	
   108	- Patching installed binaries in place.
   109	- Forking or vendoring `tauri-plugin-updater`.
   110	- Hosting patches — the manifest is a static file; bring your own storage.
   111	- Telemetry of any kind.
     1	# Changelog
     2	
     3	All notable changes to this project are documented in this file.
     4	
     5	The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
     6	and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).
     7	
     8	## [Unreleased]
     9	
    10	### Fixed
    11	
    12	- Corrected the declared minimum supported Rust version from 1.77 to 1.85. The
    13	  1.77 claim was wrong and CI's `msrv` job failed on it: `blake3` pulls in
    14	  edition-2024 crates, which no toolchain before 1.85 can parse. Reasoning
    15	  recorded in `docs/DECISIONS.md`.
    16	- The AppImage round-trip test can no longer pass vacuously. Nothing asserted
    17	  that the two fixture versions actually differ, so a generator change making
    18	  them identical would have left the whole suite green while proving nothing.
    19	
    20	### Added
    21	
    22	- `TauriInstall` — hands a verified artifact to `tauri_plugin_updater::Update`,
    23	  and the plugin registration/`Builder`. All Tauri-specific code lives in one
    24	  thin module; the flow beneath it has no Tauri dependency.
    25	- `tauri-plugin-updater-delta` — the client flow: fetch manifest, select a patch,
    26	  download it, reconstruct, verify, hand off. Both boundaries are traits
    27	  (`Fetch`, `InstallHandoff`), so the whole path is tested offline with no Tauri
    28	  runtime. `InstallHandoff::install` takes a `VerifiedArtifact`, so an unverified
    29	  install cannot be expressed.
    30	- `VerifiedArtifact` — a token obtainable only through successful minisign
    31	  verification, so the install handoff cannot be reached with unverified bytes.
    32	  It owns the verified bytes rather than a path, closing the window in which a
    33	  file could be swapped between the check and the handoff.
    34	- `client::plan_update` and the `Fetch` trait — the whole client decision path,
    35	  testable with canned responses and with no Tauri or network dependency.
    36	- `delta-release` — release-time tool that turns the previous and new installers
    37	  into a patch, digests, a minisign signature and a `manifest.json`. File-in,
    38	  file-out, no network access.
    39	- Release manifest as a **superset of Tauri's static updater JSON**: the same
    40	  `version`, `notes`, `pub_date` and `platforms` fields, with delta information
    41	  under a separate `delta` key. The full-download fallback is therefore the
    42	  official updater's own document, so the two cannot drift apart.
    43	- `try_reconstruct` — the delta path's entry point. It returns
    44	  `Reconstruction::Verified` or `Reconstruction::FallBack` and cannot fail, so
    45	  no error can escape the delta path and abort an install.
    46	- `ZstdBackend::with_expected_output_bytes` — bounds both the output and the
    47	  zstd window from the size the manifest declares, closing the allocation gap
    48	  documented in Phase 1.
    49	- End-to-end test suite: a manifest produced by the real release tool is handed
    50	  to a simulated client with nothing else, which must reach a verified artifact
    51	  from the manifest alone. Corrupt, truncated, wrong-base, unknown-backend and
    52	  wrong-signing-key cases each assert a fall back to full download.
    53	- `release.yml` — tagged-release workflow, dry-runnable via `workflow_dispatch`
    54	  so the wiring can be exercised without cutting a release.
    55	- Shared fixtures crate, so the engine and the release tooling are tested
    56	  against byte-identical artifacts.
    57	- `patch_bytes_are_identical_on_every_platform` — pins the patch digest so
    58	  cross-platform determinism is enforced by CI rather than eyeballed once.
    59	- `docs/DECISIONS.md` — log of non-obvious decisions and the conditions that
    60	  would cause them to be revisited.
    61	- Cargo workspace with the `tauri-updater-delta-core` crate, holding the
    62	  platform-agnostic diff/apply engine.
    63	- `FileHash` and `verify_file` — BLAKE3 content hashing used to prove a
    64	  reconstructed artifact matches the published one byte-for-byte.
    65	- `PatchBackend` trait, and `backend_for` to resolve a backend from the
    66	  identifier recorded in a patch manifest.
    67	- `ZstdBackend` — the default backend, using zstd prefix-referencing (the
    68	  library equivalent of `zstd --patch-from`). Applying streams its output to
    69	  disk and stops at a configurable ceiling, so a hostile patch cannot force an
    70	  unbounded write.
    71	- AppImage round-trip test suite covering exact reconstruction plus corrupt,
    72	  truncated, wrong-base and oversized-output patches. On the synthetic fixture
    73	  a patch is 5.78% of a full download.
    74	- Project documentation: architecture, roadmap, sprint tracking and contribution
    75	  guide.
    76	
    77	[Unreleased]: https://github.com/Chahdane/tauri-updater/commits/main

It is: 312 313 > Fall back on any failure that does not call the *manifest's authenticity* into 314 > question. A signature failure is the sole case where the manifest itself is 315 > under suspicion, so no fallback path exists. 316 317 Everything else is a statement about one artifact or one transfer, and says 318 nothing about whether the release document is genuine. A signature failure says 319 the opposite. 320 321 ### Why there is nothing to fall back to 322 323 This follows directly from decision #5, the manifest-as-superset. The 324 full-download URL and the delta information live in **one document**, covered by 325 **one signature over the target installer**. So if that signature does not check 326 out, the document is untrustworthy in its entirety — including the 327 `platforms..url` a fallback would fetch from. 328 329 Falling back would download an artifact chosen by a document we have just decided 330 we cannot trust, and would then verify it against a signature from that same 331 document. It preserves the risk while presenting itself as the safe option, which 332 is worse than failing loudly: the user believes a safety mechanism engaged when 333 it did not. 334 335 ### The load-bearing condition 336 337 **This reasoning depends on the full-artifact URL and hash sharing one signed 338 document with the delta information.** That is true of schema 1 and is a 339 consequence of #5. 340 341 If a future change ever splits them — a Tauri-native manifest plus a separate 342 delta sidecar, signed independently — **this asymmetry must be re-examined**. In 343 that world a delta-side signature failure would say nothing about the 344 Tauri-native document, and falling back could be both safe and correct. The 345 conclusion would change even though the code would still compile and every test 346 would still pass. 347 348 Not a change being made. Recorded so a later refactor cannot quietly reopen the 349 question by moving the ground the argument stands on. 350 351 --- 352 353 ## 12. Depending on `tauri` means inheriting its 371 whole dependency tree's floor, and that floor will keep moving. The engine 372 crates would still build on 1.85 — only the plugin needs 1.88 — so if a low MSRV 373 ever matters more than a single workspace-wide number, the split already exists 374 along the right seam. 375 376 **How this stays honest:** the `msrv` job reads `rust-version` from `Cargo.toml`, 377 so it tests whatever is declared. It caught this drift on the branch rather than 378 after release, which is the whole reason the job exists. 379 380 --- 381 382 ## 13. Change a few 401 bytes in the main binary and every compressed byte after that point shifts — 402 different back-references, different Huffman coding, different bit alignment. The 403 uncompressed tars are nearly identical; the compressed ones share almost nothing. 404 405 The engine reuses whatever the two inputs genuinely share. Here they share very 406 little *as presented*, so a 95% patch is the correct answer to the question being 407 asked. Same format, same input, 459 different behaviour. 460 461 ### Why it is worth a decision entry 462 463 This is precisely the failure that kills adoption quietly. Someone follows 464 Tauri's own documentation, accepts the default of no password, gets an error that 465 appears to be about a password they never set, and concludes the tool is broken. 466 467 Handled in two ways: the error now names the cause and the remedy, and a test 468 pins the behaviour so a version bump in either library cannot change it 469 unnoticed. 470 471 **Revisit when:** either library changes its empty-password handling — at which 472 point the test fails and this entry explains why it was ever there. An app that 12 ships weekly at 80 MB moves roughly 4 GB per user per year, when the actual 13 change is usually a fraction of a percent of that. 14 15 ## The core decision: wrap, don't replace 16 17 **This plugin does not implement updating. It moves bytes 43 around and has no idea what an AppImage is. The only per-platform work is the 44 adapter that hands the finished artifact to the installer. 45 46 ## The flow 47 48 ```mermaid 49 flowchart TD 50 A[App checks for update] --> B[Official updater reports
version + artifact URL] 51 B --> C{Patch manifest lists a patch

This catches a corrupt patch, a corrupt base, a wrong base version 74 and a bug in the backend, all with one check. 75 4. **Handoff** passes the verified file to the platform adapter, which gives it 76 to the official updater's install step. 77 78 ### Where the base artifact comes from 79 80 Applying a patch requires the *old* artifact, and an installed app does not 81 normally keep the installer it came from. Two strategies, both planned: 82 83 - **Cache the artifact** after an update completes, so the next update has its 84 base ready. Cheap, but useless for the very first delta update and for anyone 85 who installed from the website. 86 - **Reconstruct the base** from what is on disk where the installed layout allows 87 it deterministically. 88 89 Until a base is available, the plugin simply does a full download. The design 90 never assumes the base is present. 91 92 ## The `PatchBackend` trait 93 94 Delta algorithms have genuinely different trade-offs — patch size against memory 95 use against apply speed — and the right one depends on the artifact.     docs: state the macOS delta ratio honestly, per platform
    
    Measured on a real bundle: 95.14% on macOS .app.tar.gz against 5.78% on
    Linux AppImage. Predicted in ARCHITECTURE before it was measured; the
    measurement confirms the mechanism rather than revealing a bug.
    
    gzip is a streaming format, so changing a few bytes of the main binary
    shifts every compressed byte after it. The uncompressed tars are nearly
    identical; the compressed ones share almost nothing. The engine reuses what
    the inputs genuinely share, and as presented they share very little.
    
    A single averaged ratio would overpromise on two platforms out of three, so
    the README carries a per-platform table saying plainly that macOS is
    correct but not yet worth enabling.

diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index e2e4af8..78f65fb 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -100,6 +100,30 @@ These bytes are reproduced identically on Linux, macOS and Windows — asserted
 CI rather than compared by eye, since `zstd-sys` compiles a vendored C library
 and MSVC is the likeliest place a divergence would hide.
 
+### Ratios differ enormously by platform — read this before adopting
+
+| Platform | Artifact | Measured | Status |
+| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
+| **Linux** | `.AppImage` | **5.78%** | Works as intended |
+| **macOS** | `.app.tar.gz` | **95.14%** | Correct, but saves almost nothing yet |
+| **Windows** | NSIS `.exe` / `.msi` | not measured | Unknown |
+
+macOS is measured on a real bundle built by `cargo tauri build`, not a fixture,
+and the result is honest: **a delta currently saves about 5% of a macOS
+download.** The artifact is gzip-compressed, and gzip is a streaming format, so
+changing a few bytes of the main binary shifts every compressed byte after it.
+The two artifacts share almost nothing *as presented*, even though the
+uncompressed tars are nearly identical.
+
+The fix — delta the uncompressed tar and reproduce the gzip layer
+deterministically — is designed but not built. Until it lands, enable this on
+Linux and treat macOS as correct-but-not-yet-worthwhile. Windows uses compressed
+containers too, so expect it to look more like macOS than Linux until measured.
+
+Reasoning and the route out are in [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md) #13.
+A single averaged "delta updates for Tauri" number would overpromise on two
+platforms out of three, so this table exists instead.
+
 ## Installation
 
 Not published to crates.io or npm yet. Once it is, this section will carry the

 **How this stays honest:** the `msrv` job reads `rust-version` from `Cargo.toml`,
 so it tests whatever is declared. It caught this drift on the branch rather than
 after release, which is the whole reason the job exists.
+
+---
+
+## 13. Delta is correctness-only on macOS until the tar layer is addressed
+
+**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active, tracked as Phase 4/5 work
+
+Measured on the real example app, two versions built by `cargo tauri build` and
+published by `delta-release`:
+
+| Platform | Artifact | Patch | Full | Patch as % of download |
+| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+| Linux | `.AppImage` (synthetic fixture) | 393,782 | 6,815,744 | **5.78%** |
+| macOS | `.app.tar.gz` (real bundle) | 3,860,122 | 4,057,308 | **95.14%** |
+
+macOS saves almost nothing. This was predicted in ARCHITECTURE before it was
+measured, and the measurement confirms the mechanism rather than revealing a bug.
+
+### Why
+
+`.app.tar.gz` is **gzip-compressed**, and gzip (DEFLATE) is a streaming format:
+its output at any point depends on everything that came before. Change a few
+bytes in the main binary and every compressed byte after that point shifts —
+different back-references, different Huffman coding, different bit alignment. The
+uncompressed tars are nearly identical; the compressed ones share almost nothing.
+
+The engine reuses whatever the two inputs genuinely share. Here they share very
+little *as presented*, so a 95% patch is the correct answer to the question being
+asked. The question is wrong, not the answer.
+
+### The fix, already sketched
+
+Delta the **uncompressed tar**, then reproduce the gzip layer deterministically
+so the reconstructed `.app.tar.gz` is byte-identical to the published one — which
+it must be, because the signature covers those exact bytes (#6). That is more
+involved than it sounds: it requires pinning the compressor's parameters so the
+same input always yields the same output, and confirming Tauri's bundler is
+reproducible in the same way.
+
+Phase 4/5 work. **Not a Phase 3 blocker** — a 95% patch exercises the install
+path exactly as a 5% one does, so it does not weaken the end-to-end proof at all.
+
+### What this means for adopters
+
+State ratios per platform, never as one number:
+
+- **Linux / AppImage** — the intended case, and the engine performs as designed.
+- **macOS** — correct but not yet worth enabling; wait for the uncompressed-tar
+  work.
+- **Windows** — unmeasured. NSIS `.exe` and `.msi` are also compressed
+  containers, so expect something closer to macOS than Linux until measured.
+
+A single "delta updates for Tauri" claim that quietly averages these would
+overpromise on two platforms out of three.
+
+---
+
+## 14. rsign2 and the `minisign` crate disagree about empty passwords
+
+**Decided:** 2026-08-12 · **Status:** active
+
+A key produced by `tauri signer generate --password ""` **cannot be loaded by
+`delta-release` at all** — not with an empty password, not with any password. It
+fails with `Wrong password for that key`, which is a baffling thing to read about
+a key that has no password.
+
+This is not a Tauri bug. Tauri signs with that key perfectly well.
+
+### The divergence
+
+Tauri's CLI signs with **rsign2**; this project uses the **`minisign` crate**.
+Both write the same file format, and the key's header confirms the encryption
+fields are populated (`kdf_alg: Sc`, non-zero salt). They differ in one place:
+
+- **rsign2** runs its KDF over the password whatever it is, including `""`.
+- **`minisign`** skips encryption entirely when the password is empty:
+  `if !password.is_empty() { sk = sk.encrypt(password)? }`.
+
+So rsign2 writes a key encrypted under the empty password; `minisign` then reads
+it without decrypting and the checksum check fails. Same format, same input,
+different behaviour.
+
+### Why it is worth a decision entry
+
+This is precisely the failure that kills adoption quietly. Someone follows
+Tauri's own documentation, accepts the default of no password, gets an error that
+appears to be about a password they never set, and concludes the tool is broken.
+
+Handled in two ways: the error now names the cause and the remedy, and a test
+pins the behaviour so a version bump in either library cannot change it
+unnoticed.
+
+**Revisit when:** either library changes its empty-password handling — at which
+point the test fails and this entry explains why it was ever there. The
+longer-term fix is to sign with rsign2 directly, guaranteeing key compatibility
+with whatever Tauri's CLI produces.

Author:     Abderrahmane Chahdane <a.chahdane@gmail.com>
AuthorDate: Wed Aug 12 15:43:14 2026 +0100
Commit:     Abderrahmane Chahdane <a.chahdane@gmail.com>

    test(e2e): add the reproducible two-version build script
    
    Builds both versions with cargo tauri build and publishes them with
    delta-release — the same code path as a real release, nothing hand-crafted.
    
    The fixture-difference check is on the MAIN BINARY, not the tarball. Two
    versions differing only in metadata would make every downstream assertion
    vacuous, which is the appimage_pair trap arriving through a different door.
    The script aborts rather than producing artifacts that could pass emptily.
    
    Generates its signing key per run into the output directory, and restores
    tracked config on exit so a failed run cannot leave a generated key in the
    working tree.

diff --git a/examples/desktop-app/e2e/build-versions.sh b/examples/desktop-app/e2e/build-versions.sh
new file mode 100755
index 0000000..1849ec4
--- /dev/null
+++ b/examples/desktop-app/e2e/build-versions.sh
@@ -0,0 +1,107 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Build two real versions of the example app and publish them with delta-release.
+#
+# Everything the end-to-end needs, produced the way a real release would be:
+# `cargo tauri build` for the bundles, `delta-release` for the patch, the
+# digests, the signature and the manifest. Nothing here is hand-crafted.
+#
+#   ./e2e/build-versions.sh [output-dir]
+#
+# Output (default /tmp/delta-e2e-build):
+#   v1.0.0/DeltaUpdaterExample.app          the installed app under test
+#   v1.0.0/DeltaUpdaterExample.app.tar.gz   the base artifact for the patch
+#   v1.0.1/…                                the release
+#   patch.zst, manifest.json                published by delta-release
+#   key, key.pub                            generated per run, never committed
+#
+# The signing key is generated fresh each run into the output directory. A
+# test-only private key living in the repository is the same hazard class as a
+# test-only HTTP surface that ships: safe by intent, dangerous by accident.
+#
+# Note the password. `tauri signer generate --password ""` produces a key this
+# tooling cannot read — Tauri's CLI uses rsign2, which runs its KDF even over an
+# empty password, while delta-release uses the minisign crate, which skips
+# encryption when the password is empty. See docs/DECISIONS.md.
+
+set -euo pipefail
+
+OUT="${1:-/tmp/delta-e2e-build}"
+APP_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
+ROOT="$(cd "$APP_DIR/../.." && pwd)"
+KEY_PASSWORD="e2e-test-password"
+MAIN_BINARY="Contents/MacOS/delta-updater-example"
+
+ARCH="$(uname -m)"; [ "$ARCH" = "arm64" ] && ARCH="aarch64"
+case "$(uname -s)" in
+  Darwin) PLATFORM="darwin-$ARCH" ;;
+  Linux)  PLATFORM="linux-$ARCH" ;;
+  *)      echo "unsupported platform: $(uname -s)" >&2; exit 1 ;;
+esac
+
+rm -rf "$OUT"; mkdir -p "$OUT/v1.0.0" "$OUT/v1.0.1"
+
+echo "==> generating a signing key (this run only)"
+cargo tauri signer generate --ci --password "$KEY_PASSWORD" \
+  --write-keys "$OUT/key" --force >/dev/null 2>&1
+export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY="$(cat "$OUT/key")"
+export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD="$KEY_PASSWORD"
+
+# Restore the tracked config whatever happens, so a failed run cannot leave the
+# repository holding a generated public key.
+cleanup() { git -C "$ROOT" checkout -- "$APP_DIR/tauri.conf.json" "$APP_DIR/Cargo.toml" 2>/dev/null || true; }
+trap cleanup EXIT
+
+build_version() {
+  local version="$1"
+  echo "==> building $version"
+  python3 - "$APP_DIR" "$version" "$OUT/key.pub" <<'PY'
+import json, sys, re, pathlib
+app_dir, version, pub_path = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
+conf = pathlib.Path(app_dir, "tauri.conf.json")
+cfg = json.loads(conf.read_text())
+cfg["version"] = version
+cfg["plugins"]["updater"]["pubkey"] = pathlib.Path(pub_path).read_text().strip()
+conf.write_text(json.dumps(cfg, indent=2) + "\n")
+
+cargo = pathlib.Path(app_dir, "Cargo.toml")
+cargo.write_text(re.sub(r'^version = "[^"]+"$', f'version = "{version}"',
+                        cargo.read_text(), count=1, flags=re.M))
+PY
+  ( cd "$APP_DIR" && cargo tauri build --features e2e-control >/dev/null 2>&1 )
+  local bundle="$ROOT/target/release/bundle/macos"
+  cp -R "$bundle/DeltaUpdaterExample.app" "$OUT/v$version/"
+  cp "$bundle/DeltaUpdaterExample.app.tar.gz" "$OUT/v$version/"
+}
+
+build_version 1.0.0
+build_version 1.0.1
+
+# The fixture-difference discipline, at the layer that matters. Different
+# metadata wrapped around an identical binary would make every downstream
+# assertion vacuous, so this is checked on the MAIN BINARY, not the tarball.
+old_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$OUT/v1.0.0/DeltaUpdaterExample.app/$MAIN_BINARY" | awk '{print $1}')"
+new_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$OUT/v1.0.1/DeltaUpdaterExample.app/$MAIN_BINARY" | awk '{print $1}')"
+if [ "$old_hash" = "$new_hash" ]; then
+  echo "FATAL: the two versions have an identical main binary." >&2
+  echo "       Every end-to-end assertion below would pass vacuously." >&2
+  exit 1
+fi
+echo "==> main binaries differ: ${old_hash:0:16}… vs ${new_hash:0:16}…"
+
+echo "==> publishing with delta-release"
+cargo build -q --release -p tauri-updater-delta-release --manifest-path "$ROOT/Cargo.toml"
+"$ROOT/target/release/delta-release" \
+  --platform "$PLATFORM" \
+  --version 1.0.1 --from-version 1.0.0 \
+  --previous-installer "$OUT/v1.0.0/DeltaUpdaterExample.app.tar.gz" \
+  --new-installer      "$OUT/v1.0.1/DeltaUpdaterExample.app.tar.gz" \
+  --installer-url "http://127.0.0.1:0/DeltaUpdaterExample.app.tar.gz" \
+  --patch-url     "http://127.0.0.1:0/patch.zst" \
+  --patch-out     "$OUT/patch.zst" \
+  --manifest      "$OUT/manifest.json"
+
+echo
+echo "==> ready in $OUT"
+echo "    platform: $PLATFORM"
+echo "    main binary v1.0.0: $old_hash"
+echo "    main binary v1.0.1: $new_hash"
